references.text: Direct fulfillment of the serpent's promise: the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked. This shows what it actually meant to have 'eyes opened.'
The Lord God confirms that humans have become like one of us in knowing good and evil, showing that the serpent's words in 3:5 contained an element of truth.
The morning star's desire to ascend and make himself equal to the Most High mirrors the serpent's promise to be like God, revealing the fundamental nature of pride.
The prince of Tyre sets his heart as the heart of God and says, 'I am a god.' This reflects the temptation in Genesis 3:5 to become like God.
The child (Immanuel) will learn to reject evil and choose good, reflecting the theme of knowledge of good and evil from Genesis 3:5.
Jesus calls the devil a liar and the father of lies. This directly comments on the serpent's half-true promises in Genesis 3:5.
Paul refers to the serpent's deception of Eve with his cunning, fearing that the minds of believers may be corrupted away from sincerity toward Christ.
Parallel about 'open eyes' and knowledge of God: Balaam receives it through humility, while Adam and Eve seek it through disobedience.
Theological contrast: Job affirms that only God knows the way of wisdom, exposing the lie in Genesis 3:5 that humans can become like God.
Parallel about 'striving to know': Hosea shows the right path (faith and obedience), while Genesis shows the false path (self-exaltation).
